title: It Won't Last Much Longer
author: Ryan Holiday
summary: Ryan Holiday writes a brief Stoic meditation on the impermanence of childhood's small magical moments — the brief window when a pull-out couch in a hotel room is genuinely thrilling, when a dollar popsicle is real motivation, when bedtime stories are wanted. Drawing on Shakespeare's 'Out, out, brief candle,' Holiday names the dynamic plainly: children grow into cynicism and experience, and those childhood enthusiasms depart without announcement. There is no final exciting car wash and no last bedtime story recognized as the last; they simply slip away. The Stoic move Holiday makes is one of acute present attention: the father who knows this window is closing does not mourn it in advance but enjoys it completely and lets the child's joy be infectious. The piece is a characteristic Holiday compression — a single Stoic idea applied to fatherhood with maximum economy of means. The practical call is simple: appreciate the leverage while you have it, take the trips while you can, blow their minds while they still think you can, and catch the moments before they slip away unnoticed.
points: Childhood's magical moments are not permanent fixtures but a brief and closing window — the excitement about car washes, bedtime stories, and dollar popsicles will end without announcement, and the father who knows this treats those moments differently.

Holiday's Stoic framing is anti-sentimental: the right response to impermanence is not to grieve in advance but to be fully present and let the child's joy be genuinely infectious rather than bittersweet.

The leverage a father has to shape, delight, and connect with his children diminishes gradually and invisibly — there is no moment where a child declares they no longer need you in the same way; it just becomes true.

Taking the trips, blowing their minds, catching the moments — these are the practical imperatives that follow from accepting impermanence: urgency without anxiety, full presence without clinging to what is already passing.
The article's deliberate brevity mirrors its argument: the season is short, so the message should be direct, and the right response is action rather than extended reflection on what cannot be held.
